query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the multi‐phase eutectic HEA, mechanical wear continuously disrupts the naturally forming protective oxide film at elevated temperatures. This exposes vulnerable interphase boundaries—especially where the soft fcc and the hard bcc (or B2) lamellae meet—making these sites more susceptible to rapid localized corrosion. The resulting corrosion further degrades the phase interfaces, reducing their mechanical integrity and thereby accelerating wear in a self‐reinforcing, coupled degradation cycle.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar microstructure (alternating soft and hard phases) that initially has a protective surface oxide layer formed under ambient or lower temperature conditions.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., sliding or abrasion) and a corrosive environment (e.g., oxidizing species with possible chloride ions) at an elevated temperature (around 700°C).
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (≈700°C) in a corrosive medium under dynamic mechanical loading. A controlled baseline comparison should include tests with only wear (in an inert environment) and only corrosion (static conditions) at the same temperature to isolate the synergistic effect.
generation.structural_mediator: The interphase boundaries between the coexisting phases (e.g., the junctions between the soft fcc and hard bcc/B2 regions) and the transient protective oxide film on the alloy surface.
generation.mechanism: Wear mechanically removes or thins the protective oxide layer, which leaves electrochemically active interphase boundaries exposed. These exposed boundaries are preferentially corroded under the aggressive high-temperature environment. The corrosion process weakens the phase interfaces, which in turn makes the material more susceptible to further wear. This continuous feedback loop accelerates the overall degradation rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: The combined action of wear and corrosion will lead to a higher total material degradation (in terms of mass loss and surface damage) than that observed in isolated wear or isolated corrosion tests. Specifically, both the wear rate and corrosion pit density are expected to be significantly higher compared with the matched baseline alloy that is either not exposed to mechanical disruption or is in an environment that permits the oxide film to remain intact.
generation.baseline: A matched alloy sample subjected separately to (a) wear in an inert environment to maintain the oxide film and (b) static corrosion at the same elevated temperature without mechanical disruption.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies under conditions where elevated temperature promotes both a dynamic oxide film formation and its mechanical disruption, and where the microstructure is characterized by distinct phase boundaries (as in typical eutectic HEAs). Below the critical temperature or in an environment where the oxide layer is stabilized (e.g., via additional coatings), the synergistic degradation is expected to be significantly reduced.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of wear and corrosion to the overall degradation remain uncertain, as do the thresholds at which oxide removal and interphase boundary weakening become critical. Variability in microstructural features may also affect the onset and rate of the synergistic degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples. One set is left with the naturally forming oxide film; the other is pre-treated with a stable, adherent oxide or protective coating that resists mechanical removal. Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear and corrosion tests at elevated temperature. Also include control tests involving only wear (in inert atmosphere) and only corrosion (without mechanical intervention).
measurements: Corrosion pit density and depth (via surface microscopy)
Integrity and thickness of the oxide film (using XPS or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the stabilized oxide (or pre-treated coating) do not show a significant reduction in the accelerated wear-corrosion degradation compared to untreated samples, or if the combined wear-corrosion tests do not yield significantly higher degradation metrics than the sum of the individual wear-only and corrosion-only tests, then the proposed mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

Remarkable Wear Resistance in a Complex Concentrated Alloy with Nanohierarchical Architecture and Composition Undulation

Abstract: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
